Structural: a POINTER COPY is a fourth, zero-cost way to keep block 1's post-store reload — h1 is instruction- AND register-identical to the target from the prologue through block 1's if/else (13/49),

frontier.hypothesis: h1's 13 closes entirely if blocks 2/3's base takes a0 and their byte takes v1 — the target's assignment for an instruction stream the build already reproduces exactly.
frontier.mechanism: The build's base inherits v1 because base 1 dies at block 1's store and v1 is then the cheapest free register; the target's allocator picked a0 for the base, which frees the scheduler to hoist the `lui`/`addiu` pair above that `sb`. Both are legal, so the difference is an allocno-priority tie (global.c orders by reg_n_refs/live_length and breaks ties by the hard-register preference each pseudo accumulated from its copies), not a shape difference. s11 proved no PLACEMENT of the base reaches it.
frontier.next_probe: Attack the priority inputs rather than the placement: dump greg.fn for h1 (s11/dump.sh + slice.py are wired) and read the two pseudos' conflict lists, preferences and live lengths side by side, then change the REF COUNTS — e.g. blocks 2 and 3 reading the flag through the base a second time inside the arms, or the loop's `p` traffic re-spelled so `p`'s allocno is ordered differently — and re-read with sbs.py. The instrumented cc1's BB2_PRIO_DEBUG/BB2_ALLOC_DEBUG hooks (tools/gcc-2.7.2/cc1, per [[instrumented-cc1-location]]) print the priority order directly and would settle in one run which pseudo is allocated first.

frontier.hypothesis: The pointer-copy reload mechanism, being free, may also let the 9-point base structure keep its reload — i.e. h1's mechanism crossed with s10's two-variable base structure rather than with its single re-assigned handle.
frontier.mechanism: s11 only ever crossed the copy handle with base structures that give block 1 the mask's base. The 9-point form (`ptr` for mask+block 1, `ptr2` re-assigned for blocks 2 and 3) reaches the target's three bases but loses block 1's reload; h1 keeps the reload but leaves the blocks-2/3 swap. The two failures are in different regions of the function, so the cross has not actually been measured.
frontier.next_probe: Cross the copy handle with every s10 base structure the ledger records (z1's single re-assigned pointer, zz5's two variables, w3's single base) — i.e. add `ptr2 = ptr;` (or a third handle used only for the block-1 read) to each, holding everything else fixed. 6-8 forms, one probe.py run.

frontier.hypothesis: The third addend-0 base has no redundancy-free spelling at all, which makes the classification question a ruling, not a search.
frontier.mechanism: s11 closed the last open route: a direct symbol reference cannot produce an addend-0 base (it folds `%lo` per access), so a third base requires a third pointer-local ASSIGNMENT. Either that assignment re-assigns a live variable a value it already holds (the construct s10 flagged, T1/T2 failures) or it introduces a further single-assignment pointer local to the same byte, which a human writing this function would not do either — and those measure 23 (three locals), 18 (dedicated third) and 13 (four locals, i5), never 9.
frontier.next_probe: If s12/s13's attack on the h1 allocation tie does not close the function, the honest next step is a `ruling-request` naming BOTH constructs precisely — the redundant re-assignment AND the multi-single-assignment-handle alternative — with this measured impossibility argument attached, rather than another sweep of the same space.
